lesson.title: The TCP Window: How Much Data Can Be In Flight
lesson.summary: The TCP window is the receiver-advertised field that states how many bytes beyond the last acknowledgment it is currently willing to accept, implementing the general sliding window idea directly in the TCP header.
lesson.body:
The general sliding window idea is that a sender is allowed to have a bounded amount of unacknowledged data outstanding at any moment, rather than sending one unit, stopping, and waiting for confirmation before sending the next. TCP's window field is the concrete number, carried in every single segment header, that states exactly how large that bound currently is for this particular connection.

More precisely, the window field is a 16 bit value, extendable to larger values through the window scale option on high bandwidth connections, advertised by the receiver in every segment it sends. It states how many bytes beyond the current acknowledgment number the receiver is currently willing to accept and buffer. That defines the sender's allowed sending range at any given moment as everything from the last acknowledgment number it received up to that acknowledgment number plus the advertised window. This is specifically a receive window, it reflects the receiver's available buffer space, nothing about the capacity of the network path in between.

A worked numeric trace shows how this behaves. Suppose a server's receive buffer holds 4,000 bytes and starts out empty. During the handshake it advertises a window of 4,000 alongside acknowledgment number 1001, using the same numbers as the earlier handshake example. The client may now send up to 4,000 unacknowledged bytes, sequence numbers 1001 through 5000, without waiting for any intermediate acknowledgment. Say the client sends two segments of 1,500 bytes each, covering sequence numbers 1001 through 2500 and 2501 through 4000. That is 3,000 bytes now in flight, leaving 1,000 bytes of window still unused. If the server's application has not yet read any of that data out of the buffer, then when the server sends its acknowledgment, acknowledgment number 4001 confirming both segments arrived, it must also shrink its advertised window down to 1,000, since its 4,000 byte buffer now holds 3,000 bytes the application has not yet consumed, leaving only 1,000 bytes of room.

The window slides forward as data is both acknowledged on one side and consumed by the application on the other. If the server's application then reads and clears out those 3,000 buffered bytes, the server's next segment, even a bare acknowledgment carrying no new data, can advertise a window of 4,000 again, even though the acknowledgment number itself is still 4001, simply because buffer space has opened back up. That is the sliding part of sliding window: both edges of the allowed range, the acknowledged floor and the window extended ceiling, move forward independently as data gets confirmed on one side and consumed on the other.

It is worth flagging a distinction early, since it is easy to conflate the two: the window described here is entirely about the receiver's buffer capacity. TCP also maintains a separate limit, the congestion window, kept by the sender based on its own inferred sense of network conditions, and the amount of data actually allowed in flight at any moment is the smaller of the two. The receiver side limit described in this chapter, and the reason it exists, is exactly what the next chapter, flow control, is built around.
